compute.body: Computer and peripheral-equipment output growth rose materially to 12.0%, and capacity utilization reached 84.5%. Semiconductor and electronic-component output still grew faster, at 15.3%, but that rate fell materially and utilization declined to 74.4%. The production-growth gap has narrowed even as computer equipment operates at substantially higher utilization. Reuters reported, citing sources, that TSMC tightened China AI-chip curbs as new U.S. rules closed a manufacturing loophole. Access to particular advanced chips can therefore tighten even while aggregate semiconductor utilization eases.
compute.headline: Computer equipment accelerates as semiconductor growth and utilization cool

economic_impact.body: Nonfarm-business productivity grew 2.1% and real output 2.3%, compared with 0.6% growth in real hourly compensation; unit labor costs rose 2.4%. These aggregates show continued gains in output per hour without a comparable increase in real pay, but they do not identify the source. Reuters reported that Federal Reserve official Jefferson said AI was boosting inflation and that its productivity effect may come in the future. His comment reinforces the need not to treat current aggregate productivity growth as evidence of a distinct AI contribution.
economic_impact.headline: Productivity outpaces real pay, while AI attribution remains unresolved

finance.body: Borrower strain fell materially to 25.8, while lender strain rose slightly to 20.9. Borrowers still register more strain, but the gap between the two sides has narrowed. The Chicago Fed NFCI also decreased slightly to -0.48, while its three-month change declined materially to 0.07. The measures point to easing borrower pressure rather than uniform improvement across financing channels.
finance.headline: Borrower strain falls, but lenders do not share the improvement

grid_storage.body: The active interconnection queue totals 2,061 GW, including 552.7 GW of storage, but only 24.2% has reached executed-agreement or construction stages. Historical conversion provides a harder benchmark: just 13% of the 2000–2020 queue cohort reached operation. Grid operators have filed large-load interconnection reforms at FERC, placing process changes on the regulatory agenda. Those filings address how major new users connect, but they do not alter the current gap between queued and operating capacity.
grid_storage.headline: Most of the 2,061 GW interconnection queue remains at earlier stages

macro.body: The physical buildout remains substantial. Output grew 15.3% for semiconductors and electronic components and 12.0% for computers and peripherals. Available project records show 1,556 data-center sites in development, equal to about half the operating count. The electricity system illustrates why a large pipeline is not the same as delivered capacity: 2,061 GW is in active interconnection queues, but only 24.2% has reached executed-agreement or construction stages, and just 13% of the 2000–2020 queue cohort reached operation. Deployment is less extensive among businesses. Current AI use stands at 24.6%, compared with 28.6% expecting use within six months. Adults ages 18–64 report some generative-AI use at a much higher rate of 60.8%, although the consumer and business measures are not directly comparable. EE Times reported that Palo Alto Networks expanded into enterprise AI through a $4.5 billion deal. That move reflects supplier competition for enterprise demand, not proof that adoption is accelerating. The market now presents a mixed signal. The AI Equity Index edged up to 32.5 and sector trading pressure eased, but the share of covered companies with positive one-year returns fell materially to 60.8%, while the median return declined to 8.7%. Economy-wide productivity and real output grew 2.1% and 2.3%, respectively, while real hourly compensation rose 0.6%. These measures remain positive in aggregate, but they do not isolate a distinct AI contribution.
macro.headline: The physical pipeline remains large, while business use and market gains are less broad

market.body: The AI Equity Index rose slightly to 32.5, while average sector trading pressure eased to 40.7. Beneath those top-line readings, the share of covered companies with positive one-year returns fell materially to 60.8%, and the median return declined to 8.7%. The aggregate signal improved modestly, but participation in gains and typical performance both weakened.
market.headline: The aggregate AI market signal edges higher even as gains become less broad

power.body: Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.5%, nearly twice the 1.8% increase in total retail demand, while retail prices are up 5.1%. Net planned generation additions through the pipeline horizon total 227.6 GW, but planned supply is not delivered capacity. Utility Dive reported that PJM was urged to delay its base-capacity auction until data centers were cut from the forecast. The request does not establish that PJM’s forecast is overstated; it shows that data-center assumptions are consequential and disputed in capacity-market planning.
power.headline: Commercial demand outpaces total demand as data-center forecasts come under dispute

water.body: County-level drought exposure increased slightly under both measures. Among campuses with county data, 264, or 17.7%, are in counties containing some D2-or-worse drought area. The more concentrated screen now includes 201 campuses, or 13.5%, in counties where at least one-quarter of the area is D2 or worse. Both screens now point in the same direction, although they describe surrounding drought conditions rather than campus water demand or site-specific availability.
water.headline: Both county drought screens move higher for data-center campuses

editorial_briefing.style_reference: AI Macro is a research platform that examines the development of the U.S. AI economy from capital investment and physical construction through deployment, adoption, and economic results. It uses publicly available data to relate corporate and market activity to the physical systems required to support the buildout. It evaluates the extent to which that investment produces durable economic value and how its effects are transmitted through the broader U.S. economy.

body.text: The AI Equity Index edged up to 33.4, and average sector trading pressure eased to 40.0. Beneath that improvement, the share of covered companies with positive one-year returns slipped to 59.3%, and the median return fell materially to 7.3%. Recent reports offer a similarly mixed picture: Bloomberg reported that Best Buy raised guidance on demand for computing and AI glasses, while Morningstar said Dell’s record quarter lifted estimates but lowered its fair-value view because of AI-cycle risk. Those reports show firm demand in selected businesses, while the equity measures show less broad participation.

headline.text: The aggregate AI equity signal improves while company-level gains narrow

body.text: The Chicago Fed NFCI moved up slightly to -0.44, while its three-month change increased materially to 0.10. Lender strain also edged up to 21.0. Yet corporate bond-market distress declined slightly to 0.24, leaving a mixed picture: financial conditions tightened at the margin without a parallel increase in the bond-distress measure. Bloomberg reported that DoubleLine’s Cohen became more favorable toward AI debt after a selloff. That reflects one investor’s changing risk assessment, not a broad reopening of credit appetite.

headline.text: Financial conditions tighten at the margin while bond distress eases

body.text: Computer and peripheral-equipment output growth rose materially to 22.9%, overtaking semiconductor and electronic-component growth, which fell materially to 13.5%. Capacity utilization moved in opposite directions: computer utilization fell to 80.6%, while semiconductor utilization rose to 80.3%. The two industries now operate at nearly the same utilization rate even though their output growth has diverged sharply.

headline.text: The production lead shifts to computer equipment as utilization converges

body.text: Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.5%, nearly twice the 1.8% increase in total retail demand, while retail electricity prices are up 5.1%. Net planned generation additions total 227.1 GW through the pipeline horizon, but planned supply is not delivered capacity. Utility Dive reported that TVA touted a $1.7 billion data-center deal under a new large-load tariff. The agreement is a concrete sign of utility contracting for a major load, but one deal does not resolve the timing of the broader generation pipeline.

headline.text: Commercial power demand outpaces the total as TVA reports a tariff-backed data-center deal

body.text: Operating storage now has a weighted average duration of 2.8 hours, and 45.7% of capacity has at least four hours of duration; both measures improved slightly. The active interconnection queue remains 2,061 GW, but only 24.2% is in executed-agreement or construction stages. Utility Dive reported that FERC approved a MISO plan to speed its legacy interconnection study process. The change addresses processing, but it does not by itself move the large early-stage queue into construction.

headline.text: Operating storage gets slightly longer while most queued capacity remains early-stage

body.text: Among campuses with county drought data, 231, or 15.5%, are in counties containing some D2-or-worse drought area. The stricter screen—counties with at least one-quarter of their area at D2 or worse—now includes 127 campuses, or 8.5%. Both readings fell materially. This reduces the current geographic exposure count, though county drought conditions do not measure campus water use or site-specific supply.

headline.text: County drought exposure falls materially for tracked campuses

body.text: Information-processing investment growth accelerated materially to 22.7%. Across the nonfarm business sector, productivity grew 2.1% and real output 2.3%, while real hourly compensation rose 0.6%. Spending on information-processing assets is expanding rapidly, but the broader results remain more modest and do not establish how much, if any, came from AI.

headline.text: Information-processing investment accelerates as productivity continues to outpace real pay
Information-processing investment and computer output accelerate before the broader payoff is clear

paragraphs.text: Capital spending and equipment production have accelerated. Information-processing investment growth reached 22.7%, while computer and peripheral-equipment output growth rose materially to 22.9%, above the 13.5% rate for semiconductors and electronic components. Utilization moved toward the same level from opposite directions: computers fell to 80.6%, while semiconductors rose to 80.3%. Strong output growth is therefore not accompanied by uniformly rising utilization.

The electricity system continues to separate announced scale from delivered capacity. Commercial demand is growing 3.5%, compared with 1.8% for total retail demand, and retail prices are up 5.1%. Net planned generation additions total 227.1 GW, while the active interconnection queue stands at 2,061 GW; only 24.2% of queued capacity has reached executed-agreement or construction stages. Utility Dive reported TVA’s $1.7 billion data-center deal under a new large-load tariff. The deal makes large-load contracting more concrete, but it does not convert the wider generation and interconnection pipelines into operating capacity.

Broader outcomes remain mixed. Nonfarm-business productivity grew 2.1% and real output 2.3%, while real hourly compensation rose 0.6%; those aggregates are positive but do not isolate an AI contribution. The market signal is also split: the AI Equity Index edged up to 33.4, but the share of covered companies with positive one-year returns slipped to 59.3% and the median return fell materially to 7.3%. The current evidence is clearer on investment and physical expansion than on a broad economic or market payoff.
